# Legend: Color and Fill {#ggplot2-legend-color-fill}

In this chapter, we modify legend title, breaks, limits, labels and values when color or fill is mapped to categorical variables.

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this matters

Color and fill legends decode groups; keep titles plain words and show only needed breaks.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

`limits` does not filter the data. For color and fill, points outside the limits are drawn in grey (`na.value`); for shape and size they are removed, and ggplot2 warns. Use `filter()` when you mean to subset the data.
:::

```{r setup-legend-cf, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

## How to change legend colors in ggplot2 {#change-legend-colors}

We will learn to modify the following when `color` is mapped to categorical variables:

- title
- breaks
- limits
- labels
- values

```{r legc1, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

### How to create a plot with a color legend in ggplot2 {#basic-plot .unnumbered}

Let us start with a scatter plot examining the relationship between displacement
and miles per gallon from the mtcars data set. We will map the color of the points
to the `cyl` variable. 

```{r legc2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl)))
```

As you can see, the legend acts as a guide for the `color` aesthetic. Now, let 
us learn to modify the different aspects of the legend.

### How to change legend color values in ggplot2 {#color-legend-values .unnumbered}

To change the default colors in the legend, use the `values` argument and
supply a character vector of color names. Supply a color for each level of the
categorical variable that you want to display.
In the example below, `cyl` has 3 levels (4, 6, 8) and hence we have specified
3 colors.

```{r legc3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))
```

### How to change the legend title in ggplot2 {#color-legend-title .unnumbered}

In the previous example, the title of the legend (`factor(cyl)`) is not very
intuitive. If the user does not know the underlying data, they will not
make any sense of it. Let us change it to `Cylinders` using the `name`
argument.

```{r legc4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Cylinders", 
    values = c("red", "blue", "green"))
```

Now, the user will know that the different colors represent the number of cylinders in
the car.

### How to change legend limits in ggplot2 {#color-legend-limits .unnumbered}

Let us assume that we want to change the groups shown in the legend: instead of
examining the relationship between mileage and displacement for all cars, we want
the legend to list only cars with at least 6 cylinders. One way to do this
is to filter the data using `filter` from dplyr and then visualize it.
Instead, we will use the `limits` argument to set the legend range; the data
itself is not filtered.

```{r legc5, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    limits = c("6", "8"))
```

The legend now represents only 6 and 8 cylinders. The four-cylinder cars are
not dropped: they stay on the plot but are drawn in grey, the default
`na.value` for values outside the limits. If you want to remove them from the
data, use `filter(cyl >= 6)`. Supplying numbers instead
(`limits = c(6, 8)`) also works but adds the warning "Continuous limits
supplied to discrete scale"; character values avoid it.

### How to change legend labels in ggplot2 {#color-legend-labels .unnumbered}

We can modify the labels in the legend using the `labels` argument. Let us 
change the labels to `Four`, `Six` and `Eight` in the next example. Ensure that
the labels are intuitive and easy to interpret for the end user of the plot.

```{r legc6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"),
    labels = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'))
```

### How to reorder or hide legend items in ggplot2 {#color-legend-breaks .unnumbered}

When there are a large number of levels in the mapped variable, you may not 
want the labels in the legend to represent all of them. In such cases, we can 
use the breaks argument and specify which levels to show in the legend. In the
example below, we use the `breaks` argument to ensure that the labels in the
legend represent two levels (4, 8) of the mapped variable.

```{r legc7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    breaks = c("4", "8"))
```

`breaks` controls which keys appear in the legend: here only 4 and 8 cylinders
are listed. It does not change the data, and because the values are named,
every point keeps its colour, including the six-cylinder cars that no longer
have a legend key. With unnamed values, the colours are matched to `breaks`
instead, so the unlisted group would turn grey.

### How to combine color legend options in ggplot2 {#putting-it-all-together .unnumbered}

```{r legc8, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Cylinders",
    values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    labels = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'), limits = c("4", "6", "8"),
    breaks = c("4", "6", "8"))
```

## How to change legend fill colors in ggplot2 {#change-legend-fill-colors}

We will learn to modify the following using `scale_fill_manual()` when `fill` is mapped to categorical variables:

- title
- breaks
- limits
- labels
- values

### How to create a plot with a fill legend in ggplot2 {#plot .unnumbered}

Let us start with a scatter plot examining the relationship between 
displacement and miles per gallon from the mtcars data set. We will map `fill`
to the `cyl` variable. 

```{r legc9}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22)
```

As you can see, the legend acts as a guide for the `fill` aesthetic. Now, let 
us learn to modify the different aspects of the legend.

### How to change the fill legend title in ggplot2 {#fill-legend-title .unnumbered}

The title of the legend (`factor(cyl)`) is not very intuitive. If the user
does not know the underlying data, they will not make any sense of it. Let us
change it to `Cylinders` using the `name` argument.

```{r legc10}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Cylinders", 
    values = c("red", "blue", "green"))
```

### How to change legend fill values in ggplot2 {#fill-legend-values .unnumbered}

To change the default colors in the legend, use the `values` argument and
supply a character vector of color names. Supply a color for each level of the
categorical variable that you want to display.
In the example below, `cyl` has 3 levels (4, 6, 8) and hence we have specified
3 colors.

```{r legc11}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))
```

### How to change fill legend labels in ggplot2 {#fill-legend-labels .unnumbered}

We can modify the labels in the legend using the `labels` argument. Let us 
change the labels to `Four`, `Six` and `Eight` in the next example. Ensure that
the labels are intuitive and easy to interpret for the end user of the plot.

```{r legc12}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"),
    labels = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'))
```

### How to change fill legend limits in ggplot2 {#fill-legend-limits .unnumbered}

Let us assume that we want to change the groups shown in the legend: instead of
examining the relationship between mileage and displacement for all cars, we want
the legend to list only cars with at least 6 cylinders. One way to do this
is to filter the data using `filter` from dplyr and then visualize it.
Instead, we will use the `limits` argument to set the legend range; the data
itself is not filtered.

```{r legc13}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    limits = c("6", "8"))
```

The legend now represents only 6 and 8 cylinders. The four-cylinder cars are
not dropped: they stay on the plot but are drawn in grey, the default
`na.value` for values outside the limits. If you want to remove them from the
data, use `filter(cyl >= 6)`. Supplying numbers instead
(`limits = c(6, 8)`) also works but adds the warning "Continuous limits
supplied to discrete scale"; character values avoid it.

### How to reorder or hide fill legend items in ggplot2 {#fill-legend-breaks .unnumbered}

When there are a large number of levels in the mapped variable, you may not 
want the labels in the legend to represent all of them. In such cases, we can 
use the breaks argument and specify which levels to show in the legend. In the
example below, we use the `breaks` argument to ensure that the labels in the
legend represent two levels (4, 8) of the mapped variable.

```{r legc14}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    breaks = c("4", "8"))
```

`breaks` controls which keys appear in the legend: here only 4 and 8 cylinders
are listed. It does not change the data, and because the values are named,
every point keeps its colour, including the six-cylinder cars that no longer
have a legend key. With unnamed values, the colours are matched to `breaks`
instead, so the unlisted group would turn grey.

### How to combine fill legend options in ggplot2 {#putting-it-all-together-1 .unnumbered}

```{r legc15}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, fill = factor(cyl)), shape = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Cylinders",
    values = c("4" = "red", "6" = "blue", "8" = "green"),
    labels = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'), limits = c("4", "6", "8"),
    breaks = c("4", "6", "8"))
```


## Exercises

1. Recolor cylinder groups with `scale_color_manual(values = ...)`.
2. Rename legend entries with the `labels` argument.
3. Show only 4- and 8-cylinder levels with `breaks` and justify vs `limits`.
